span.p: Purged — DB row gone, stored object destroyed

div.style: display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
Guest paths filter on GuestSearchService.isPubliclyVisible — removedAt null,
isPublic != FALSE, project untrashed and is_visible_to_public != FALSE — so only
Public reaches /api/guest/feed and /api/guest/audios/{audioCode}.
/api/guest/audio/{audioCode}/stream skips that check: AudioStreamAPI filters on
removed_at alone, so Hidden and Project-hidden bytes still reach anonymous callers.
Staff GET /api/audio reads AudioReadCache.getAllActive over findAllByRemovedAtIsNull,
so all three substates show. project:update defaults to visibilityCascade=NONE and
leaves is_public alone; CASCADE drives the media to Hidden too.

div.style: display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
One nullable column decides it: removed_at NULL is active, NOT NULL is trash,
indexed by idx_audio_removed_at. Trash list is GET /api/audio/trash over
findAllByRemovedAtIsNotNull.
delete, restore, getTrash and purge all require audio:delete, which ADMIN alone
holds by default — absent from Role.EMPLOYEE_DEFAULT_PERMISSIONS, but grantable
per user. requireAdminRole re-checks that same authority, not ROLE_ADMIN, and
plain DELETE never calls it.
Restore while the parent project is trashed, and purge of a still-live row, both
fail 400 AUDIO_VALIDATION_ERROR.
Trash is not invisible to staff: restore, purge and GET /api/audio/{audioCode}/stream
use findByAudioCode with no removed_at filter.

div.style: display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
deleteStoredFile runs only when s3Service.isOurS3Url(url) — an externally hosted
audio_file_url is left alone. Purge is not the only step that destroys bytes:
PATCH /api/audio/{audioCode} with a replacement file deletes the old object, and
ProjectService.purge sweeps findAllByProject — every child, trashed or not.
